hints: Look at the right-hand side of the graph where substrate concentration is very high. Which inhibitor curve eventually reaches the same maximum rate as no inhibitor, and which one stays much lower?

Remember that adding lots more substrate can out-compete an inhibitor only if they are fighting for the same place, the active site. If the maximum rate (Vmax) stays lowered, the inhibitor must be acting elsewhere.
walkthrough:
**Read what the curves do at high substrate**

Look carefully at the plateau (maximum rate). With inhibitor X, the rate starts slower but eventually catches up to the no inhibitor curve at high substrate concentration.

With inhibitor Y, the rate plateaus much lower and never catches up, even with lots of substrate.

**Link the pattern to inhibitor type**

A competitive inhibitor binds to the active site. Because it has a similar shape to the substrate, high substrate concentration can out-compete it, so Vmax stays the same. That matches X.

A non-competitive inhibitor binds away from the active site, at the allosteric site. It changes the enzyme shape, so adding more substrate cannot overcome it, and Vmax is lowered. That matches Y.

**Pick the correct description**

So X is competitive (binds active site, similar shape to substrate) and Y is non-competitive (binds away from active site, different shape).

Only option D describes Y correctly.

options.A: X does act as a competitive inhibitor, but competitive inhibitors bind into the active site, not away from it.
options.B: X is not non-competitive. Its Vmax is unchanged at high substrate, and non-competitive inhibitors do not have a similar shape to the substrate.
options.C: Y is not competitive. Its maximum rate stays low and cannot be restored by high substrate, so it cannot be competing for the active site.
options.D: Y lowers Vmax permanently, which is classic non-competitive inhibition by binding at a site away from the active site.
